title: The final Amen (CCC 2855–2865)
hook: the Catechism ends where prayer ends: Amen

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last four petitions: bread, forgiveness, temptation, deliverance. Your line was give, forgive, lead, deliver.

A thick book on a table. It holds the creed line by line, the sacraments one by one, the commandments, and then a long walk through prayer. Turn to its very last paragraph, and what it's talking about is one small word. Not a doctrine. Not a rule. A word said at the end of prayers, often without a thought. The Catechism of the Catholic Church closes on Amen. We've read it part by part since the start of this year, and today we reach that same last word. Today: the final Amen.
screen: `A THICK BOOK.` → `ITS LAST PARAGRAPH.` → `ONE SMALL WORD.`

segments.voice: First, what comes just before it. In the Douay-Rheims, Matthew's Our Father ends simply: "But deliver us from evil. Amen." Christians who use the King James wording go on: "For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever." At Mass, Catholics say words of praise much like these, after a short prayer by the priest. The Catechism says this praise gathers up the first three petitions, the name, the kingdom, the will, and hands them back to God. Then the Amen, which you met at Mass back on day one hundred fifteen. The Catechism quotes Cyril of Jerusalem, teaching new Christians: after the prayer, you say Amen, which means so be it, and so put your seal on everything the prayer contains. A signature at the bottom of a letter. In its final paragraph the Catechism goes one step further: the last Amen is our own yes to all seven petitions. Days ago we met Mary's yes at the angel's word. Here everyone who prays gets to say one like it. And in Revelation, Christ himself is given the name: "These things saith the Amen, the faithful and true witness." So for Catholics the word that ends the prayer is also a name for the one it goes through. Now look back. The Catechism has four parts, and we've walked them all this year: what the Church believes, how it celebrates, how it lives, how it prays. It ends with a word a small child can say.
screen: `THINE IS THE KINGDOM.` · `AMEN: SO BE IT, A SEAL.` · `OUR YES TO EVERY PETITION.` · `FOUR PARTS, ONE LAST WORD.`

segments.voice: If you pray, choose one line of the Our Father you most want to mean today, say it, and answer it with one deliberate Amen, like a signature; take another line if there's time. If you don't pray, think back over these months, one belief, one sacrament, one way of living, one prayer that stayed with you, and let them rest together.
The final Amen. The last word of the Our Father, and the subject of the Catechism's last paragraph: so be it, our yes to everything the prayer asks.
Your line: amen. Tomorrow a new part begins, with a boy locked in a tower. Go gently.

screen: `DAY 1151 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BOY IN THE TOWER.`

howItsDone: Catholics end their prayers with Amen and answer Amen many times during Mass, including when receiving Communion; at Mass, the Our Father is followed by a short prayer of the priest and then the people's words of praise to God's kingdom, power and glory.

fork.setup: you're a new Christian, hearing Cyril of Jerusalem explain the Our Father. you reach the last word. what does he tell you it does?

fork.reveal: Cyril, quoted in the Catechism: after the prayer you say Amen, which means so be it, and so you seal what God has taught you to ask.

original.note: Hebrew: amen — a word from the Hebrew scriptures; Cyril explains it as "so be it."

chat.says: What does Amen actually mean? Is it just how you say a prayer's finished?
options: It means so be it. Cyril of Jerusalem called it a seal; the Catechism calls it our yes to all we asked.
Mostly, yes; the Catechism treats it as a closing signal, like hanging up, with no meaning of its own.
It's the Latin word for peace; the Catechism says it wishes peace on everyone who prayed along.
chat.meaning: Cyril of Jerusalem says Amen means so be it, a seal on everything the prayer contains. The Catechism's last paragraph calls it our yes to the petitions.
